text: Recall, in free space, our signal travels in an ideal scenario where there are no obstacles, and as we know from high school, the power with which the signal is received depends on the transmitted power, so the power at which the signal is transmitted, the gain of the antenna at the transmitter end and the receiver. If the antenna is isotropic, so it irradiates over an angle of two pi, then the antenna gain is equal to one. If instead we get an antenna that is directive, that means it transmits over one direction, like along a sector, then the gain is greater than one. Okay, so directive antennas concentrate the power over a certain sector only, not two pi, but only a restricted angle, and since they concentrate all the power in a restricted angle, the gain is higher than one. So, if you know where your receiver is, you may want to use directive antennas, right, and concentrate the power where the signal has to go. Okay, so this is again as we said, high school material, and this is just another way to look at the attenuation of our signal. So the attenuation is.
